question_text: Find the number of 7-digit numbers that can be formed using the digits 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4.

recall_prompt: Say how you would count the arrangements of the digits 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4 into seven-digit numbers — what you count first and which formula you use.
insider_note: All seven digits are used and none is 0, so there is no leading-digit case to remove: the whole question is 7!/(3!·2!·2!) = 210. The divisor holds one factorial per repeated digit — three of them, product 24.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Count the letters and the repeats
steps.margin_note: First mark. Seven digits: 2 three times, 3 twice, 4 twice. No zero, so every arrangement counts.
lines: Seven digits: 2 three times, 3 twice, 4 twice.
No digit is 0, so every arrangement is

recall.must_convey: That there are seven digits with 2 repeated three times and 3 and 4 twice each, and no zero to exclude.
accept: seven digits, three twos, two threes, two fours, no zero
count the repeats, two three times, three twice, four twice
the digits are like a word with repeated letters, three two two
seven digits, two moodu sarlu, three rendu, four rendu
no zero so all arrangements are valid numbers

steps.why: Alike letters cannot be told apart, so swapping them does not give a new arrangement. The count of each repeated letter is what the formula divides by, so it must be found before anything else.
common_mistakes: Treating the three 2s as different digits and answering 7! = 5040.
Looking for a leading-zero case when there is no 0.

steps.label: Apply n!/(p!·q!·r!)

recall.must_convey: That the count is 7 factorial over 3 factorial times 2 factorial times 2 factorial, which is 210.
accept: seven factorial over three factorial two factorial two factorial is two hundred ten
five thousand forty by twenty four is two ten
seven factorial by three factorial two factorial two factorial two ten
divide seven factorial by twenty four

steps.why: n! counts the arrangements as if every letter were different; each group of p alike letters has been counted p! times over, so dividing by p! for each group leaves the true count.
